subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: adapting routines after early problems [Revision]
passage: I'm Baljeet, and my first month in the new city ran on chai and panic. I slept late, skipped breakfast, and by eleven the words in my notes swam. My marks on the first test showed it. One evening my roommate Sunaina said, “You look like a phone on two percent.” That stung, and it was true. So I changed three things. First, a fixed wake-up and lights-out time, written on the wall. Second, a tiffin service two lanes away that brings dal and rice at one and at eight. Third, I moved my study block to five in the morning, when the hostel is quiet, instead of the noisy evenings. It took two weeks to feel normal. By the second test I could finish a chapter without my eyes closing.

qa.q: What three changes did Baljeet make?
qa.a: Baljeet set a fixed wake-up and lights-out time, found a tiffin service two lanes away, and moved the study block to five in the morning.

qa.q: What did Baljeet feel when Sunaina said the remark about a phone on two percent?
qa.a: It stung, so Baljeet felt hurt, but Baljeet also knew it was true.

qa.q: What else could help if the new schedule still leaves Baljeet drained?
qa.a: Baljeet could talk to the warden, and if it keeps going or worries Baljeet, check with the doctor, since routine changes may not solve everything.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have seen the change?
qa.a: Sunaina probably felt relieved to see Baljeet finishing chapters, since the remark came from worry as much as from teasing.

grounding: After skipping breakfast and struggling to focus, a student sets a fixed schedule, finds a nearby tiffin service and shifts study time to when the hostel is quiet.

subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: adapting routines after early problems [Revision]
passage:
Hostel warden's note, end of September
In her first month, Ira from Room 9 skipped breakfast almost every day. She would sleep past seven and run for the bus with nothing, and her class teacher told me she was drifting off in the late-morning lectures. She also tried to study in the evenings, when the common room is at its loudest.
In the third week she came to me herself and said, “Something isn't working.” We talked it through. Since then she has changed three things. She sleeps and wakes at fixed times: lights off at eleven, up at six-fifteen. She has signed up with the tiffin service run by Ujjwal's family two lanes away, and collects breakfast on her way to the bus. And she studies from five to seven in the morning and after nine at night, when the hostel is quiet.
Her teacher says she is much more alert. She looks happier at the gate, too.

qa.a: From five to seven in the morning and after nine at night.

qa.q: What might Ira have been feeling when she said "Something isn't working"?
qa.a: Ira was probably frustrated and tired, but ready to change rather than keep struggling.

qa.q: What else could Ira do if the new routine slips?
qa.a: Check in with the warden again and adjust one thing at a time, such as the study slot, rather than dropping the whole routine.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal's family see having Ira as a customer?
qa.a: They gain a regular customer and probably feel good that their breakfast helps a student far from home.

grounding: A warden notes a student who, after skipping breakfast and struggling to focus, moves to a fixed routine, finds a nearby tiffin service and studies when the hostel is quiet.

subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: adapting routines after early problems [Revision]
passage:
Friday, week 6
Changed things this week, and it's working.
The first month here was a mess. I skipped breakfast because the mess stops serving at 7:45 and I kept waking at 7:40. By eleven, in chemistry, I couldn't follow anything. And I tried to study at night, when Parveen and everyone else on the floor watch cricket with the volume up.
On Monday I made a proper routine and stuck it on the wall. Sleep by 11, alarm at 6:30, breakfast by 7:15. I also found a tiffin aunty in the next lane who packs poha or upma, so on bad days I grab that. And I moved study to 6 to 8 in the evening, when the floor is still empty because everyone's at the ground.
Result: I actually understood the chemistry class today. Parveen asked what changed. I said breakfast.
– Santosh

qa.q: Where did Santosh find breakfast for bad days?
qa.a: A tiffin aunty in the next lane who packs poha or upma.

qa.q: How is Santosh feeling at the end of week six?
qa.a: Santosh feels pleased and relieved that the new routine is working and chemistry finally made sense.

qa.q: What else could Santosh do if a cricket night clashes with a test?
qa.a: Ask Parveen and the floor to keep the volume down that night, or study in the library.

qa.q: How might Parveen see the change in Santosh?
qa.a: Parveen notices something is different and is curious, maybe amused that the answer is simply breakfast.

grounding: Shows a student who skipped breakfast and struggled to focus changing to a fixed routine, finding a tiffin service and studying when the hostel is quieter.
